summary: Initial discovery focused on model selection tradeoffs for Cascade AI's multilingual customer support product. Key topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment, context length needs (50k tokens vs 8k), multilingual quality, tool-calling/structured output, and security/compliance. Redwood AE/SE proposed a pilot with Hosted for rapid evaluation and Dedicated for production with Private as a later option for compliance. Agreed next steps: send model comparison and benchmarks, schedule infra deep-dive.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. We have Priya from our SE team with me. How are you all?
[00:06] Evelyn Carter: Hi Jordan, thanks. Good, excited to chat. We have Marco and Sofia on as well.
[00:12] Sofia Alvarez: Hey. Quick note, we're short on time so if we can focus on the model questions and deployment options that would be ideal.
[00:20] Jordan Kim: Totally, we'll keep it tight. Priya, quick intro?
[00:23] Priya Singh: Hi all — Priya, Redwood SRE/SE — I cover performance, latency, and private deployments.
[00:28] Marco Diaz: Great. To frame it: Cascade AI is building a multilingual customer support assistant for mid-market telco customers. We need very long context (we're seeing use cases up to 30-50k tokens for conversation history + docs), high accuracy in Spanish/Portuguese/English, and we want structured tool-calling for ticket creation and DB lookups.
[00:45] Jordan Kim: Perfect, that helps. Couple of high level questions for qualification: what's your exec timeline and primary metric for success — is it latency, cost per query, or accuracy?
[00:54] Evelyn Carter: Timeline is Q4 production for a pilot, broad rollout next year. Primary metric is response quality (esp multilingual) and reliability; latency target is sub-800ms for short replies, but for the large 30k+ context calls we're okay with higher p99s as long as they are predictable. Cost is important but secondary.
[01:17] Priya Singh: Good to know. For 30k-50k contexts we typically recommend model families with long context variants — open models like Mistral Long or LlamaX-L has long-context options, and Redwood also supports custom chunking + prefix caching to reduce cost. But tradeoffs exist between quantization/accuracy and long-context throughput.
[01:37] Marco Diaz: When you say prefix caching, is that the KV cache reuse you're talking about? How does that work with dynamic conversation where users reference new docs?
[01:45] Priya Singh: Yeah, prefix/KV caching stores previous activations so repeated prefixes don't get recomputed; for dynamic docs we recommend a hybrid approach — cache the base convo, stream embeddings/lookup results for doc access, and fall back to full context when necessary. There's some heuristics to keep cache hit rates high.
[02:02] Jordan Kim: On hosting options — given you want pilot in Q4, many customers start on Redwood Hosted to move fast, then evaluate Dedicated for predictable throughput and Private if they have compliance (SOC2, data residency). Do you have any security requirements that would force private now?
[02:17] Sofia Alvarez: We're SOC2 in flight but not certified yet; however some enterprise customers will require VPC or on-prem eventually. For the pilot, hosted is fine if data handling is clear.
[02:27] Jordan Kim: Makes sense. We'll send our security pack and SOC2 roadmap.
[02:30] Evelyn Carter: Appreciate it.
[02:33] [03:00] Marco Diaz: A couple of model questions: how do Redwood's verifed profiles compare across open models for multilingual performance? Is there a preferred family?
[03:10] Priya Singh: Short answer: depends. For multilingual quality at 8k context, families like Mistral and LlamaX variants do well; for 32k-64k we point to long-context tuned versions — some are natively trained for long sequences, others use sliding window + retrieval. We have per-model perf/quality profiles we can share. Tradeoff is often that very long-context modes increase compute cost and memory, so Dedicated helps.
[03:34] Jordan Kim: Also, tool-calling — you mentioned structured output. Our platform needs JSON schema enforcement for ticket creation. Does Redwood support function/tool calling?
[03:44] Priya Singh: Yes — Redwood supports tool-calling and structured output; you can use function-like signatures or schema-guided outputs. We can also validate outputs server-side and apply deterministic rerun policies. Some open models have quirks producing malformed JSON — we usually add a validation + fallback step.
[04:03] Sofia Alvarez: That fallback step — is it part of Redwood or do we code it in our app?
[04:07] Priya Singh: A bit of both: Redwood offers structured output features and post-processing hooks; many customers do lightweight app-side validation too. We'll share an example flow in the benchmark doc.
[04:16] [05:00] Evelyn Carter: On latency vs cost tradeoffs — curious about batching and quantization. If we quantize aggressively to save cost, how much accuracy hit do you typically see on multilingual tasks?
[05:12] Priya Singh: Depends on the model and quant format. 4-bit quantization can be quite good for decoding in many open models with minimal quality loss, but for fine-grained multilingual nuance, especially for less-represented languages, there's sometimes a drop. We recommend doing A/B tests on your prompt set. Our Redwood Optimize recommendations can suggest quant profiles per workload.
[05:33] Marco Diaz: Do you have customers using 50k contexts in production? That seems large.
[05:39] Priya Singh: There are a few — they typically use mixture of retrieval, chunking, and long-context models. Dedicated clusters with high memory GPUs or sharded KV cache are common. We also recommend hybrid routing: short queries -> fast small model, long queries -> long-context model to balance cost.
[05:57] Jordan Kim: Maybe to make it concrete: for pilot we could suggest three model configs — 8k multilingual base for latency-sensitive paths, 32k long-context tuned model for deep convo + docs, and a retrieval-augmented small model for simple queries. We'll include estimated tokens-per-call cost.
[06:16] Sofia Alvarez: That sounds good. One more: how do you handle PII and logs? We need retention controls and optional non-retention for certain customers.
[06:24] Jordan Kim: Redwood has configurable retention, optional opt-out for logging at route level, and integrations with KMS for keys. We'll include our retention policy doc.
[06:32] [07:00] Evelyn Carter: Great. On benchmarks — would you run a small benchmark on our prompt set? We can share 300 representative user interactions across languages.
[07:09] Priya Singh: Yes, we'd love that. We can run quality/latency/cost comparisons across 3-4 models. For benchmark privacy we can run it on Redwood Hosted with data controls or set up an isolated Dedicated bench. Which do you prefer?
[07:21] Marco Diaz: Initially hosted is fine as long as the strings are handled per your non-retention option. If pilot goes well, we'll ask for Dedicated.
[07:30] Jordan Kim: Noted. We'll propose hosted pilot with Dedicated production path.
[07:34] [08:00] Sofia Alvarez: A technical question: our infra needs VPC peering and private endpoints — what's Redwood's Private offering look like?
[08:09] Priya Singh: Redwood Private provides a customer-controlled control plane with VPC connectors, private endpoints, and optionally on-prem packaging. For high-security customers we do bring-your-own-key (BYOK) via KMS/HSM and audit log streaming. There's some deployment lead time (weeks) vs Hosted but it's production-ready.
[08:27] Sofia Alvarez: Lead time is okay as long as Dedicated can bridge.
[08:31] Jordan Kim: Yep — Dedicated is usually faster to ETA for reserved capacity.
[08:36] [09:00] Marco Diaz: About integration — we need streaming responses for partial replies and tool-calling mid-generation. Can Redwood stream tokens and interleave tool outputs?
[09:11] Priya Singh: You can stream partial outputs and we support callback-style tool invocations. There's also support for function-calling semantics where the model returns a structured tool call that your app executes and then streams back the result. Some open models differ on how reliably they follow the call; our runtime can enforce schema-level checks and fallback to a deterministic parser.
[09:33] Evelyn Carter: Excellent. Any limitations on number of concurrent streams?
[09:37] Priya Singh: Limits depend on plan; Hosted has soft quotas, Dedicated gives you reserved concurrency. We'll include recommended cluster sizes for your target concurrency.
[09:47] [10:00] Jordan Kim: Quick tangent — competitors. Were there providers you're evaluating?
[10:03] Sofia Alvarez: We looked at OpenAI for model quality, Anthropic for safety, and some infra teams considering Vertex for GCP integration.
[10:12] Jordan Kim: Good context. Redwood's angle is production economics and flexible hosting. For safety we have guardrails and eval tooling — Priya will show example evals in the follow up.
[10:22] Priya Singh: We'll include a safety / eval pack and a simple reproducible evaluation harness.
[10:27] [12:00] Marco Diaz: Let's talk pricing briefly — for the pilot what's realistic spend? We want a small bench test and maybe 10k calls.
[12:10] Jordan Kim: For Hosted pilot, depending on model choice, ballpark is $X to $Y per 1k tokens — we'll send a model-specific estimate. For Dedicated you'd commit monthly but get better unit economics for heavy usage.
[12:25] Evelyn Carter: Understood. Send the estimate.
[12:29] [15:00] Priya Singh: I'll summarize technical tradeoffs we discussed: 1) Use 8k low-latency model for short convo paths; 2) 32k-50k long-context tuning for doc-heavy interactions; 3) Retriever/RA for cost reduction; 4) Quantization profiles for cost/throughput; 5) Tool-calling with server-side validation.
[15:46] Marco Diaz: That summary is helpful. Also we have multilingual edge cases (Brazilian Portuguese, Mexican Spanish), do you have evaluation data around dialect robustness?
[15:55] Priya Singh: We recommend you include dialect-specific prompts in the benchmark; we'll also add a few open-models known for better latin-american spanish coverage.
[16:03] Jordan Kim: Ok, action items and timeline — Jordan to send pricing and model matrix by Aug 2, Priya to run bench on the 300 prompts once received and share results in ~3 business days, then infra deep-dive week of Aug 9. Does that work?
[16:19] Evelyn Carter: Yes. One ask: include example JSON schemas for ticket creation so our engineers can review.
[16:24] Priya Singh: Will do. We'll also attach a sample flow for schema enforcement.
[16:29] [20:00] Sofia Alvarez: Big picture — we're comfortable starting Hosted pilot; Dedicated/Private later depending on enterprise deals. Also, please make any model recommendations explicit — we want the top 3 picks and why.
[20:39] Jordan Kim: Understood, top 3 with rationale will be part of the matrix.
[20:44] Marco Diaz: Any red flags we should watch for?
[20:47] Priya Singh: Watch for degraded performance when you push naive long-context on models not designed for it — memory blowouts and high p99s. Also, some open models produce hallucinated tool calls — we mitigate with schema validation and retrieval.
[20:59] Evelyn Carter: Good notes.
[21:03] [25:00] Jordan Kim: Anything else from you all?
[25:05] Marco Diaz: Not from me.
[25:06] Sofia Alvarez: No.
[25:07] Evelyn Carter: No, thanks.
[25:10] Jordan Kim: Thanks everyone. We'll send the docs: model comparison matrix (link: internal), security pack (link: internal), benchmark template (link: internal). Looking forward to the infra deep dive.
[25:22] Priya Singh: Thanks all.
[25:25] [45:00] Transcript end.

Notes: Transcription had occasional mis-recognition of model names (e.g., "LlamaX" transcribed as "Llama X"), some speaker overlaps. Shared artifacts mentioned: model_comparison_matrix.xlsx (internal link), security_pack_v2.pdf (internal link), benchmark_template.csv (internal link).

Recap / Next steps: Jordan to send matrix + pricing; Priya to run bench and share recommendations + quantization notes; schedule infra deep dive week of 2027-08-09.
